title: 'The Substance' is in poor taste, anyone else feel this way?

commenti.body:
Yes, I agree. I think it genuinely appeals to our prejudices, without criticising them, and determines by the end that the worst thing, the terrible impact of ageism, is ugliness. It may parody the male gaze but it also just uses it. There were so many bottoms and stomachs; Margaret & Demi were both under real pressure to look good, and then neither actor really gets to \*do\* enough to give them agency or power over this presentation of their images.

I also think what it's satirising is untrue. Women don't resent each other for being younger or older. Both parties know it's never easy. By the last 20 minutes I'd signed out, anyway.

First of all, you’re making a really precarious argument. Using your logic, we could say that a deformed humanoid monster in any movie is “inspired” by the elephant man, which is just dumb, sorry. And the movie is satire, it’s about the currency of beauty, and when it comes down to it, the message is actually very similar to that of Elephant Man.

I think the point was to say that society makes older women feel like Elephant Men themselves. It’s how they begin to see themselves because of unrealistic beauty standards they’ve been told they should maintain in order to still feel deserving of life, much less love.

This is the role of references in literature/film. You got like 95% of the way there when you said what the point of Elephant Man was. You’re then supposed to go that last 5% and apply it to The Substance’s themes. It’s not there just for superficial entertainment reasons.

[Literary analysis of The Substance](https://filmcolossus.com/the-substance-explained-2024)

Look up a film called Leviathan (1987), if anything what you’re referencing looked more like than anything else, more so than even John Carpenter’s The Thing.

Major influences included Cronenberg-Ian body horror as per the director. I really doubt they were specifically referencing anybody from real life like Joseph Merrick.

How are you so sure that the movie is making fun of the monster instead of turning the camera towards us for judging the monster for not representing the beauty we expect and for used to? We even see her looking in the mirror in a manner of self acceptance after becoming the monster after chasing that unattainable youth the whole film. Finally now that she is this person she made the choice to just accept herself as who she is. 

I think it says a lot about the audience that we would find or be offended by the grotesque nature of the monster just like the audience in the theatre at the end. You are literally pointing out the point of The Elephant Man while missing the same point in The Substance. It’s just subverted in the sense that people only care about Elisabeth/Sue if she’s young and beautiful instead of the person she really is.
[removed]
[removed]

Society isn’t in the substance. Or at least it’s so abstracted and heightened it’s meaningless to talk about in relation to the real world. It hates women for conforming to sexist systems way more than the systems themselves

I totally agree, I also felt it was a really crass final stretch (the less it's said about the eyeball-tit, the better, ugh) and that the treatment of the deformed creature kind of betrayed the film's intentions because it felt like transforming into that was obviously a way to punish Elisabeth and Sue's 'greedy' behavior, but at the same time the creature itself was kind of gentle and naive (precisely like John Merrick) and just wanted to be accepted, so the way it was treated felt undeserved and cruel, maybe a bit disconnected from what came before. I think that the director really didn't know how to end the film and kept throwing things at the screen to see what stuck, including as many references to Kubrick and Cronenberg as she could, but I feel that using a Cronenbergian-Lynchian monster as the resolution was very unimaginative and obvious. The film could've taken so many interesting and fun paths after the end of the second act when Sue starts falling apart (for a minute while I was watching I thought that the 'better version' of Sue would end up being a not-quite-good-looking-but-charming middle-aged man, and that the film would make a commentary on how everyone is more forgiving of men's aging than women's, since men's careers in show business have virtually no expiration date.) But in the end I feel they took the easy way out which was to try and shock the audience through intensity (loud music, increasingly grotesque images, sparays of blood...) rather than through finding a more creative, consistent and actually subversive way to resolve the conflict and giving us something really different (we've seen deformed Cronenbergian creatures too many times at this point.) This was kind of a frustrating watch. I laughed at the introduction of the shareholders though.

Bingo. 

I think the point is also that beauty can be just as isolating as being disfigured. Elizabeth has a hard time truly connecting with people throughout the movie.  The old classmate she nearly goes on a date is clearly in love with a idealized non existent version of her.  She ends up an old lonely isolated outcast.  

Then as Sue every relationship professional or otherwise is portrayed as entirely superficial and fake with the entire focus being on her body as an object.  Despite KNOWING all of this (they are the same) the fame and attention she receives is addictive and intoxicating to the point that it literally kills her.

Wow people are so close to getting it and then just fall short.  Yes it's parodying the male gaze, yes it's doing so by using it and that's the entire point.  It was there to titillate but if you think the purpose was for the viewer to just go "oh wow that's sexy" with no deeper thought I dunno what to tell you. This movie isn't very subtle with its themes.

It's a body horror film. It clearly has its own meanings; however, you're being intellectually dishonest by ignoring the fact that the creature was designed in a grotesque way to shock audiences. That's one of the primary reasons I (and many others) went and saw the film, we've been repeatedly hearing about how 'shocking' the ending was. Then the ending is just a reference to the Elephant Man with grossness dialed up to 11, e.g. when the creature vomits a tit. It's just stupid. If you're going to reference a real person in an effort to shock audiences, then I may as well be purchasing a ticket to go be disgusted by Merrick in a Victorian freak show. Do you genuinely not see the callousness of this?
Did you even read what I said? Have you even seen the Elephant Man? The similarities and references go beyond the monster's appearance.
Did you even see the substance?

It is extremely unlikely that the head shape, speech impediment, limp, etc were all accidental. The act of covering their face with a mask and the shot of the monster looking at itself in the mirror were also in Elephant Man.

There are so many similarities it's difficult for me to not view this as a reference, especially considering the director of the Substance says that Lynch was an inspiration for her: [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coralie\_Fargeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coralie_Fargeat)

>How are you so sure that the movie is making fun of the monster

Where did I say this?

>turning the camera towards us for judging the monster for not representing the beauty we expect and for used to?

It's a body horror film. It has a message, but the creature at the end is designed to disgust and shock audiences. It's referred to as '*Monstro* Elisasue' in the movie, they are referencing Joseph Merrick and then calling the creature a monster.

>I think it says a lot about the audience that we would find or be offended by the grotesque nature of the monster just like the audience in the theatre at the end.

Got it, so the people who ran the freak shows where Joseph Merrick was displayed weren't in the wrong? They were pointing out the flaws of society!

Yes.

>Using your logic, we could say that a deformed humanoid monster in any movie is “inspired” by the elephant man

Why would you even say this? You blatantly and intentionally ignored all of the clear references and similarities I pointed out.

>the point is also that beauty can be just as isolating as being disfigured

I really hope this isn't true because that is one of the most asinine things I have ever heard.

Hi OP. I love your post and think it's important. Here are some of my thoughts:

 You said:

"However, the Elephant Man was a real person, Joseph Merrick. His story is extremely sad. He was treated like a monster and displayed in freak shows as a result of his deformities. He was just as cognizant as you and me, he was fully aware of his situation. He wanted to love and connect with other people but most of society treated him as if he was an abomination."

Exactly. He was treated like a monster but he wasn't a monster. In the same way aging women are treated like monsters in a freak show - but we aren't. 

Our humanity is ignored and our natural signs of aging are treated as though they are hideous deformities and we are paraded around in freak shows (social media, tabloids etc.). Our 'deformoties' are highlighted, magnified and exploited. We are shamed, shunned and isolated. 

The beauty industry and plastic surgeons then  commodify our pain, just as the freak show does, and pressures us to inflict bodily harm under the guise of 'curing our deformity.' After undergoing endless painful, radical body modifications and unnecessary medical procedures such as face lifts, fillers, breast implants, butt implants, botox etc. we are then called "freaks and monsters" and shamed, shunned and isolated once again for our 'deformities.' 

Sometimes, we no longer recognize ourselves in the mirror or contract life threatening infections or develop other adverse reactions to said procedures. We do all this, just so we can be accepted, and 'pass' as 'normal.' We do all this, so we can meet YOUR beauty standards, while who we are and our innate value is entirely disregarded and ignored. And we are asked to do all of this, endure all of this, with a smile on our face, or we are shamed, shunned and isolated (the mask on Elisasue). 

What you are missing is that Elisasue wasn't a monster. She was a physical representation of the horror these impossible standards create. She is a social creation (hence the line: she is my most beautiful creation). In reality, Elisasue is just a woman. A person. Entitled to respect and love. A person who deserves respect and value and community. The concept of a freak is a social construct. It's not real. There are no freaks. There are only people. That is the point OP. Women are people, not freaks. This shouldn't be a radical concept but it is. 

You said: 

"That is the entire point of Lynch's film.** It's about society's inhumane treatment of a genuinely good person, simply because they were unwilling to look past the superficial. The overall message of the film is that Merrick was not a monster, he was a human being who deserved respect."

Exactly OP. Exactly. And that is the entire point of The Substance.

“Satire is a genre of the visual, literary, and performing arts, usually in the form of fiction and less frequently non-fiction, in which vices, follies, abuses, and shortcomings are held up to ridicule, often with the intent of exposing or shaming the perceived flaws of individuals, corporations, government, or society itself into improvement.[1] Although satire is usually meant to be humorous, its greater purpose is often constructive social criticism, using wit to draw attention to both particular and wider issues in society.”
For real, clearly spoken by someone who is not disfigured.
Dude, why are you so fixated on this has to be a copy and paste of Elephant Man?  Your analysis of this film is just straight up ass backward, kind of like the ending of this film.

Lmao this is not the first time this theme has been explored in media.  David Foster Wallace explores the same theme in the boom Infinite Jest through the character of Joelle Van Dyne a woman so beautiful she chooses to wear a veil because her beauty causes ingenue jealousy from women and uncontrolled desire from men.

It's really not hard to imagine how being stunningly beautiful and only appreciated for your outer beauty could be isolating and lonely.

But you couldn't even grasp themes to a fairly simple film so I don't begrudge you for not understanding.

This movie is satire. If it references Elephant Man, it’s doing it satirically. That’s the point. It’s about women’s inhumane treatment of a genuinely good person (themselves), simply because they are unwilling to look past the superficial. And this is due to societal standards and the pressure put on them (and that they put on themselves) to be flawless. That’s the joke. If an aging, beautiful woman has some minor flaws she may as well be the elephant man. 

It’s not making fun of Merrick the man. It’s referencing Elephant Man the movie. Ipso facto; It’s referencing the message of Elephant Man the movie, in my opinion, in a subversive and hilarious way.
You sound super judgemental. You must be fun at parties.

It's not just a body horror film that's parading an elephant man esque figure in bad faith. It's a critique of the extreme beauty standards we put on aging women. The film is so extremely unsubtle about this I'm having trouble understanding of you missed it? Consider the themes of Lynch's film to how our society can treat aging women and you have your answer.

The ending also heavily references Carrie, a movie where a woman is tricked into going on stage in order to be humiliated, and retaliates by destroying the audience. 

It's almost as if the director is on the side of the monster and critical of her treatment by society

Are... you serious?

You can't imagine, in our current patriarchal society, a woman not being taken seriously because of her beauty? I mean, in lesser ways this kind of idea has been explored in media in a number of ways.

It also literally happens to women all of the time.

There are other movie “creatures” with similarities in looks, speech, limp, shyness, etc.  There are other movies where a transformation occurs and looking in the mirror happens literally every time.  The POV through the mask shot is also a bit of a trope. 

But given all that, even if the movie was meant to directly reference Lynch’s Elephant Man, you missed the point I think.  As others have pointed out, it’s made to represent how women *feel*.  Making you feel like they were being put on display as freaks is the intention.
You’re getting downvoted to hell in this thread, just give it up my brother

Did you not notice the very, very clear references to other films from the 1970s and 80s, like *The Fly,* *Carrie,* and *The Shining,* among others? The film uses images and tropes from (mostly horror) classics as part of its vocabulary for communicating the subjective experience of extreme body dysmorphia, identification with a misogynist male gaze, self-loathing, etc. Being a woman in our society, it's saying (in an unserious but earnest way), especially an aging woman, especially in Hollywood, is like being trapped in a Lynchian (or Cronenbergian, or Carpenter…ian) nightmare.
What makes you think I give two fucks about that

They are in the wrong for calling Merrick a monster, just like the audience is wrong for only valuing Sue only for her beauty. That is the point. They were pointing out the flaws of society. You literally see Elisabeth in the beginning being fired just for being too old.

The movie called the creature a monster with a title card referring to it as ‘Monstro’. A creature that is a clear reference to the Elephant Man, who famously shouted ‘I am not a monster!’ in that film.

Yeah, when she’s “beautiful” people accept her when she can’t accept herself. But when she’s a “monster” only then she can accept herself. The movie is calling her a monster in the sense in that the audience is calling her a monster. Even is she isn’t.

Man, how are you here still not getting the point with all the precise responses that completely negate your premise? It is really interesting to not understand something by such a wide mark, but I'm assuming a) you're a dude, b) you're young, and c) the movie wasn't made for you.

This movie triumphs in swinging for the fences on showing society that we are the monsters for our misogyny, expectations, judgement, and retiring of "real people" that are "treated like monsters".

That's not what they said though, not being taken seriously and something being so isolating that it's comparable to being horribly disfigured aren't the same thing.

If you are beautiful you are desirable by both sexes. And you can call these emotions superficial, but they are very real. Romantically they lead to a higher percentage of people developing strong feelings for you, but even in day to day life they make others want to be around you. Attractive people are perceived as more trustworthy, competent, etc - this benefits them in all aspects of their lives, including at work.

I feel like the vast majority of people in this thread are grossly misinterpreting my argument here. The movie can make important social commentary and still be somewhat callous regarding how it references the Elephant Man, these are completely separate things.

All I am saying is that if the creature was a reference to the Elephant Man (and I'm fairly confident it was, given all the evidence I've provided), it seems somewhat callous to use his visage in an effort to shock audiences. It's even more callous to then refer to that creature as a 'monster' directly within the title/transition cards of the film itself, considering the entire point of the Elephant Man film was that Joseph Merrick was "not a monster!" (which he shouted in the train station).

I didn't miss the themes of the movie, I am talking about an entirely different thing. The movie can have important social commentary and still be somewhat callous in the way it references Elephant Man. I have no idea why you're misinterpreting my argument.

It’s the same point of The Elephant Man but instead of ugliness it’s beauty. Unless you think beauty can only be a good thing. Or rather, what society thinks is beautiful.

If it's a metaphor regarding the way women treat themselves, I don't see anything wrong with that. If it's supposed to be a metaphor about society's treatment of older women (which other commentors have stated), I'd find that in poor taste, as older women aren't even remotely treated as poorly as people with severe deformities.

I took Monstro to be (at least partially) symbolic of plastic surgery addiction tbh. Women in the public eye are pressured heavily by both the industry and the press to use tasteful cosmetic procedures so they can look "great for 40!" or "ageless at 50!" - but as soon as it becomes remotely obvious, or they've gone a little too far, then they are botched, destroyed their beauty, not letting themselves age gracefully etc etc. 

Monstro reminded me of the way Jocelyn Wildenstein has been endlessly in the showbiz news cycles because the press knows she gets a decent mixture of pity and WTF clicks. The human freak show you talk about still happens - just in grubby tabloids.

I think you're right, your explanation makes the most sense to me. Sadly most of the people in this comment section must think you lack 'media literacy' because your explanation doesn't match theirs.

If you are correct, then the Elephant Man references do make more sense to me. Someone like Jocelyn Wildenstein is treated by society in a similar way to Joseph Merrick. My only remaining reservations would be regarding the fact that plastic surgery is something you consent to and do to yourself.

Depending on how you perceived the split consciousness, Elisabeth consented to everything that happened to her. IMO, she was on a reckless high as Sue, and on a comedown with painful clarity as Elisabeth. She was shown a hint of what happens (with the finger), but as what naturally happens in the throes of addiciton, the high beats out the consequences. 

While initially it played out more like a typical drug addiction, the moment that Elisabeth first calls The Substance helpline about her finger, I feel this then parallels closer to surgery addiction. She cannot live with this one consequence of her addiction, so dives deeper into it to avoid confronting it. Sue is the exciting process of getting another procedure, chasing that reveal of youth and beauty, and by the time the actual reveal happens, she has botched herself even more so and is even further removed from her original beauty. 

Eventually, after several cycles of dysmorphia and self-destruction, you lose any realistic gauge on your physical appearance. You live unrecognisably as yourself as fodder for the tabloids, all while trying to project confidence and beauty because that has been how society has determined your value. It's an incredibly tragic ending, and basically there are a lot of surgeons who should be in prison.

Even the tit has a point you're missing. All the other women on that stage were topless. There were tits everywhere. No one cared, not even in front of the kids.  The men in the hallway were trying their hardest to look at them as the women walked by. It's like, isn't this what you came for? Don't you want to see tits? All of a sudden you don't want more tits on the stage? Yes, it was definitely a (fantastic) shock. But there was meaning behind why that specific body part was chosen, imo.

I disagree, because I feel like film does indeed make the exact point you’re critiquing it for not making. 

The final act is Elisesue’s radical self acceptance. As Elisabeth continued with the substance, she isolated herself more and more because of her insecurities, rarely leaving the house or if she did covering herself in the giant yellowtrenchcoat, wearing sunglasses, trying to be invisible essentially. But as Elisasue she puts on the dress and the earring and unapologetically faces the world. As the audience rejects and attacks her she repeatedly shouts ‘It’s me! I’m the same person!’, exactly showing how the audience is unwilling to look past the superficial. Despite Elisabeth and Sue and Monstro Elisasue all being one, only Sue is valued, but they are all human beings who deserve respect.

I was thinking the same thing. I'm a college student studying freak shows and their consequences in-depth, and I know an Elephant Man when I see one. Quick disclaimer I did not like this movie and that already puts me in a minority. I don't like body horror or the deformed body as horror at all, and regardless of the themes of the movie, that's still what it was. It was a body horror meant to shock and disgust. Was it also about Hollywood beauty standards? Sure. But Monstro Elisasue was, quite literally, straight out of a freak show.

  
Monstro Elisasue dons a dress, some earrings, and makeup. You know what they did to the "freaks" in freak shows? You guessed it, dressed them up as "respectable citizens" to both juxtapose their clothing with the ugliness of their bodies and, at the same time, highlight their apparent humanity. Freak shows were big on saying "look, these freaks are people to!" just as the movie does. But the assertion of the freak's humanity does not negate the entertainment of consuming it. If anything, it adds to the experience. We, watching the freak, realize that Monstro Elisasue is human and feel sympathy for her, but we still laugh, cringe, and gawk at the spectacle before us. This was all intentional. This is exactly what freak shows did. The fact that Elisasue's face was based off a real person is just the cherry on top of an undeniable freak show experience. 

  
One of the foundational essays on disability studies asserts that "while stories rely upon the potency of disability as a symbolic figure, they rarely take up disability as an experience of social or political dimensions" (Narrative Prothesis and the Materiality of Metaphor by Mitchell and Snyder). Everything from Oedipus to common sayings like "going in blind" or "blind trust" is a material metaphor, that is, using something physical to explain something incorporeal.  These comments, who are all bashing you by asserting the themes of the movie (ignoring the ultimate goal of those themes as a body horror) prove the assertion. Elisasue does not exist outside of a metaphor for the aging of women and Hollywood's body standards. Her disabilities, callbacks to the Elephant Man, and body exists in a vacuum not at all representing disability itself but rather the grotesque nature of being an aging woman. And for some reason, according to the comments, that moves her beyond criticism.

  
And for the record, aging women are treated horribly but... perhaps we shouldn't equate that to the elephant man or the other disabled men and women in freak shows. It's not... it isn't the same. Maybe read a bit about what they went through before saying someone like Demi Moore is in a similar position...

  
anyways I hope you read this and find it interesting, and if you're interested in some resources on freak shows or disability studies you should let me know!
